I want to put something uncomfortable on the table, and I will try to be fair about it. The claim we keep hearing is that any work made with a community automatically carries their consent. Admittedly, that is often true, and I do not want to overstate the objection. But consent given at the start of a five year project is not the same as consent to whatever the project became. While the intention is almost always good, the ethics are handled at the beginning and then never revisited. I take issue with one specific thing here: we describe the participants as collaborators in the catalogue and as subjects in the archive, and we do it in the same week. That is not a small inconsistency. It is where the argument has its blind spot, and it is the part I would want an artist to have an answer for before the work travels.

A quick word on how these sessions run, because it makes a difference to how useful they are. We are not looking for consensus at the end, and nobody should feel they have to win. What we do ask is that when you disagree, you name the exact thing you disagree with, rather than the person or the whole position. If somebody has made three claims and you find two of them compelling, say so first, and then take the third one apart. It sounds like a small courtesy. It is not. In my experience it is the difference between a discussion that moves and one where two people spend forty minutes defending things nobody actually attacked. And if you find yourself with no common ground at all, that is worth saying out loud too, calmly, because it usually means the two of you are answering different questions.

Somebody asked me afterwards how I stay so calm when a question comes at me hard, and the honest answer is that I stopped hearing those questions as attacks about ten years ago. What changed was one habit. Before I respond to anything, I say back the strongest version of what the other person just said. Not the weakest, the strongest. If I can put their point better than they put it, two things happen. They relax, because they have been heard, and I find out whether I actually understood the objection or whether I was about to answer a question nobody asked. Only then do I say where I differ. It costs about fifteen seconds, and it has saved me from a great deal of unnecessary defensiveness, most of it my own.
